demos.q: What is the night currency requirement under Part 61?
demos.a: To carry passengers at night you need 3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop within the preceding 90 days, in the same category and class.

cites.tip: GACAR §61.17(a)(2). Recent flight experience at night: 3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop in the preceding 90 days to carry passengers at night.

demos.q: Minimum flight visibility for VFR in Class D?
demos.a: In controlled airspace below 10,000 ft you need 3 SM flight visibility and the 1-2-1 cloud clearance: 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal.

cites.tip: GACAR §91.165. Basic VFR weather minimums: visibility and distance-from-cloud by airspace class and altitude.

demos.q: Does approved simulator time count toward the instrument rating?
demos.a: Yes, approved FFS or FTD time is creditable toward the instrument rating, up to the limit in the aeronautical-experience table.

cites.tip: GACAR §61.89. Instrument Rating Requirements, including the aeronautical-experience credit for approved flight-simulation training device time.

crosswind.title: Crosswind & headwind
crosswind.intro: Resolve the reported wind into its crosswind and headwind components for a runway. The inputs ride the URL, so any setup is shareable.
crosswind.diagramHint: Enter runway, wind direction and speed to see the wind diagram.
crosswind.diagramLabel: Wind vector diagram. Runway {{rwy}}°, wind {{dir}}° at {{spd}} kt; crosswind {{xw}} kt from the {{side}}.
crosswind.diagramLabelCalm: Wind vector diagram. Runway {{rwy}}°, wind {{dir}}° at {{spd}} kt; crosswind negligible.
crosswind.formula: The wind angle is the signed difference between the wind direction and the runway heading (−180° to +180°). The crosswind component is wind speed × sin(angle) and the headwind is wind speed × cos(angle). A positive crosswind blows from the right; a negative headwind is a tailwind.

densityAltitude.title: Density altitude
densityAltitude.intro: Pressure altitude, ISA deviation and density altitude from field elevation, the altimeter setting and the outside air temperature. A planning aid: performance figures come from the POH/AFM.
densityAltitude.formula: Pressure altitude = field elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 27.3 ft/hPa; density altitude = pressure altitude + 118.8 ft × ISA deviation. Hot, high and humid raise it, and with it the take-off run and the true airspeed for a given indicated speed. The POH/AFM is authoritative.

tas.title: True airspeed
tas.intro: Convert calibrated airspeed to true airspeed and Mach via the ISA standard atmosphere, from CAS, pressure altitude and OAT.
tas.formula: TAS rises above CAS as the air thins with altitude and temperature: roughly TAS = CAS × √(ρ₀/ρ), about +2% per 1,000 ft. Use CAS for performance limits, TAS for navigation, and groundspeed (TAS ± wind) for timing.

glossary.title: Aviation glossary
glossary.subtitle: Plain-language definitions of the Saudi-aviation terms and abbreviations you meet across the GACAR library, the charts and the study tools. Independent and educational — always verify against the official GACA sources.

terms.def: The General Authority of Civil Aviation Regulations: the body of Saudi civil-aviation rules, organized into numbered Parts.
The General Authority of Civil Aviation: Saudi Arabia's civil-aviation regulator, and the authority Fly GACA cites and defers to.
Aeronautical Information Publication: the official manual of a state's aeronautical information — aerodromes, airspace and procedures — issued by GACA for Saudi Arabia.
Notice to Air Missions: a time-critical notice of a hazard or change (a closed runway, an unserviceable navaid) that crews must check before flight.
A routine, coded observation of the actual weather at an aerodrome, issued at regular intervals.
Terminal Aerodrome Forecast: a coded forecast of the expected weather at an aerodrome over a set period.
Automatic Terminal Information Service: a continuous recorded broadcast of essential aerodrome and weather information.
Visual Flight Rules: the rules for flying by outside visual reference, permitted only in visual meteorological conditions.
Instrument Flight Rules: the rules for flying by reference to instruments, required in instrument meteorological conditions.
Visual Meteorological Conditions: weather — visibility and distance from cloud — good enough to fly under Visual Flight Rules.
Instrument Meteorological Conditions: weather below the VMC minima, requiring Instrument Flight Rules.
The altimeter pressure setting that makes the altimeter read altitude above mean sea level, so it shows aerodrome elevation on the ground.
The altimeter pressure setting that makes the altimeter read height above a chosen datum, typically the aerodrome — zero on the runway.
The standard altimeter setting of 1013.25 hPa (29.92 inHg), used at and above the transition altitude so every aircraft shares one datum.
The altitude at or below which vertical position is expressed as an altitude referenced to QNH.
The lowest flight level available above the transition altitude; above it, level is expressed as a flight level on the standard setting.
An altitude referenced to the standard pressure setting (1013.25 hPa), expressed in hundreds of feet — FL350 is 35,000 ft.
True Airspeed: the aircraft's speed through the air mass, corrected for air density (altitude and temperature).
Indicated Airspeed: the speed read directly from the airspeed indicator, uncorrected.
The aircraft's speed relative to the ground: true airspeed adjusted for the wind.
The ratio of true airspeed to the local speed of sound; Mach 1 is the speed of sound.
International Standard Atmosphere: an agreed model atmosphere (15 °C and 1013.25 hPa at sea level) used to calibrate instruments and compare performance.
Pressure altitude corrected for temperature — the altitude the air 'feels' like to the aircraft. High density altitude degrades performance.
The altitude indicated when the altimeter is set to the standard pressure of 1013.25 hPa.
Mean Sea Level: the reference datum for altitude and elevation.
Above Ground Level: height measured from the surface directly below the aircraft.
Any defined area of land or water used for the arrival, departure and surface movement of aircraft; 'airport' usually implies added facilities.
The part of the wind blowing across the runway, at right angles to the direction of travel — the part that pushes the aircraft sideways.
The part of the wind blowing straight down the runway against the direction of travel, which shortens the ground run.
The height above the ground of the lowest cloud layer reported as broken or overcast.
The greatest horizontal distance at which prominent objects can be seen and identified.
Airspace of defined dimensions within which an air traffic control service is provided.
The ICAO classification (A to G) that sets which flight rules, services and clearances apply within a block of airspace.
Terminal Control Area: controlled airspace established at the confluence of routes around one or more major aerodromes.
Control Zone: controlled airspace extending upward from the surface around an aerodrome.
Flight Information Region: an area within which flight information and alerting services are provided.
Minimum Sector Altitude: the lowest altitude that gives a safe obstacle clearance within a specified sector around a navigation aid or aerodrome.
The four-digit transponder code assigned by air traffic control to identify an aircraft on radar.
The number painted on a runway: its magnetic alignment rounded to the nearest ten degrees, with the final zero dropped — 340° becomes 34.
The beginning of the portion of a runway usable for landing.
A landing threshold set back from the physical start of the runway; the paved area before it is not available for landing.
A defined path on an aerodrome connecting runways with aprons, hangars and other facilities.
The paved area where aircraft park for boarding, loading, refuelling or maintenance.
Pilot in Command: the pilot responsible for the operation and safety of the aircraft during flight time.
Private Pilot Licence: permits flight as pilot in command for non-commercial purposes.
Commercial Pilot Licence: permits flight for hire or reward, subject to its ratings and limitations.
Airline Transport Pilot Licence: the highest pilot licence, required to command large multi-crew aircraft in airline operations.
Instrument Rating: an added qualification permitting flight under Instrument Flight Rules in instrument conditions.
An aeromedical fitness certificate, issued by class, that a pilot must hold; the class required depends on the licence exercised.
The pilot's personal record of flights, hours and experience, used to prove currency and meet licensing requirements.
The recent-experience requirements — such as a number of take-offs and landings in a period — a pilot must meet to carry passengers or act as pilot in command.
Saudi Aviation English Language Proficiency Test: the assessment of aviation-English proficiency against the ICAO language rating scale.
Distance Measuring Equipment: a system that shows the aircraft's slant distance from a ground station.
VHF Omnidirectional Range: a ground navigation aid that defines radials an aircraft can track to or from the station.
Instrument Landing System: a precision approach aid giving lateral (localizer) and vertical (glideslope) guidance to a runway.
Area Navigation: a method that lets an aircraft fly any chosen path within the coverage of navigation aids or self-contained systems, not just station to station.

pressureAltitude.formula: Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013.25 − QNH) × 27.3 ft. The flight level is that pressure altitude in hundreds of feet.

isaTool.formula: ISA temperature = 15 °C − 1.98 °C per 1000 ft. The deviation is OAT minus that standard temperature.

altimeter.formula: QFE = QNH − elevation ÷ 27.3 hPa. Set QNH and the altimeter reads field elevation; set QFE and it reads zero on the ground.

cloudBase.formula: Convective cloud base ≈ (temperature − dew point) × 400 ft. A rough estimate for cumuliform cloud only.

mach.formula: Speed of sound a = 38.97 × √(OAT + 273.15) kt. Mach = TAS ÷ a.

climb.formula: Percent = ft/NM ÷ 60.76. Angle = atan(ft/NM ÷ 6076). Rate = ft/NM × groundspeed ÷ 60 ft/min.

turn.formula: A rate-one turn is 3°/s. Bank = atan(V × 0.0524 ÷ g); radius = V ÷ 0.0524. Rule of thumb: bank ≈ TAS/10 + 7.

runwayBar.aria: Runway margin: {{required}} m required of {{available}} m available

compassRose.aria: Compass rose: wind {{dir}}° at {{spd}} kt against each runway

windTable.empty: Enter wind and at least one runway.
windTable.formula: Each runway is resolved against the reported wind: crosswind = speed × sin(angle), headwind = speed × cos(angle).

hydroplaning.formula: Dynamic hydroplaning speed ≈ 9 × √(tyre pressure) kt for a rotating tyre. Onset also depends on water depth, tyre wear and surface texture.

runwayPerf.formula: Required = book × (1 + 10% per 1000 ft DA) × (1 + 5% per 1% upslope) × (1 + safety factor). These are conservative rules of thumb, the authoritative figures are the AFM/POH and your operator's data.

windTriangle.heading: Heading to fly
windTriangle.diagramLabel: Wind triangle diagram: heading {{hdg}}° with wind from {{wdir}}° at {{wspd}} kt gives {{gs}} kt groundspeed.
windTriangle.formula: WCA = asin(wind × sin(wind − course) ÷ TAS). Heading = course + WCA; groundspeed = TAS·cos(WCA) − wind·cos(wind − course).

greatCircle.hint: Decimal degrees; south/west negative. OERK 24.96, 46.70 · OEJN 21.68, 39.16.
greatCircle.formula: Haversine great-circle distance on a 3440 NM-radius Earth, with the initial true bearing.

oneInSixty.formula: Track error ≈ (off-track ÷ flown) × 60. Closing angle ≈ (off-track ÷ to-go) × 60. Total = track error + closing.

tod.formula: Gradient = tan(angle) × 6076 ft/NM. Distance = height ÷ gradient; rate = gradient × groundspeed ÷ 60 ft/min.

vdp.formula: VDP distance = HAT ÷ (tan(angle) × 6076). Below the VDP a normal descent to the runway is possible.

tsd.hint: Fill any two; the third is computed.
tsd.formula: distance = groundspeed × time ÷ 60. Leave one field blank to solve for it.

fuel.formula: Endurance = fuel ÷ fuel flow. Range = endurance × groundspeed. Use one consistent fuel unit (L, kg or gal).

specificRange.formula: Specific range = groundspeed ÷ fuel flow = distance per unit of fuel. Higher is more efficient.

weightBalance.formula: CG = Σ(weight × arm) ÷ Σweight. %MAC = (CG − LEMAC) ÷ MAC × 100. Load the real arms and limits from the AFM/POH.

zulu.formula: Saudi Arabia is UTC+3 (Arabia Standard Time), with no daylight saving.

airac.formula: AIRAC cycles are 28 days. Effective dates are fixed worldwide; the identifier is the 2-digit year plus the cycle number within that year.

sunTimes.noEvent: The sun does not cross this angle on this date.
sunTimes.arcAria: Sun path across the day, from sunrise to sunset.
sunTimes.formula: Computed from the sun's position for the date and place. Civil twilight is the sun 6° below the horizon. Shown in UTC and KSA local (UTC+3).

part61Currency.formula: Currency expires the recency window after the date you last completed the required recent experience (e.g. three take-offs and landings). GACAR Part 61 sets the exact period and conditions, confirm against Part 61.

medicalValidity.formula: Expiry = examination date + validity. The validity period depends on the certificate class and your age under GACAR Part 67, confirm the exact period against Part 67.

flightReview.formula: Next due = last completed + interval. GACAR sets the required interval and lookback for a flight review or instrument proficiency check, confirm against the rule.

holding.heading: Heading at the fix (°)
holding.formula: Entry sectors (standard right turns): Direct spans 180°, Parallel 110° and Teardrop 70° relative to the inbound course. A lap is two legs plus two 180° turns (~1 min each).

separation.formula: Closure = follower groundspeed − leader groundspeed. If closing, time to zero = spacing ÷ closure. ATC separation minima are set by procedure, this is the geometry only.

gaca-medical-class-2.name: GACA Class 2 medical
gaca-medical-class-2.blurb: The medical certificate a private pilot needs under GACAR Part 67, and how it differs from Class 1.
gaca-medical-class-2.intro: A Class 2 medical certificate is the aeromedical standard for private (PPL) flying in the Kingdom. It is issued under the GACAR Part 67 medical standards by a GACA-authorized examiner and sits a step below the Class 1 that commercial pilots need. This guide explains who needs a Class 2, what it covers, and where to confirm the current standards. It is an educational overview, not the regulation, so verify the requirements in GACAR Part 67 at gaca.gov.sa.

sections.p: A Class 2 medical is the minimum for exercising Private Pilot Licence privileges, and a student pilot needs a valid medical before flying solo. If you intend to fly commercially you will need the higher Class 1 instead. GACAR Part 67 sets which class each privilege requires.

Like the higher classes, a Class 2 examination covers vision, hearing, cardiovascular health, and general physical and mental fitness, judged against the Class 2 standard by a GACA-authorized aviation medical examiner. The Class 2 thresholds are generally less demanding than Class 1, but the current standards are set by GACA.
A Class 2 certificate is valid for a set period that typically shortens as you get older. The exact validity periods are in GACAR Part 67 — track your expiry so you never fly on a lapsed medical.

Class 1 is the higher standard for commercial and airline pilots; Class 2 is for private pilots. Holding a current Class 1 also satisfies the Class 2 requirement, but not the other way round. Match your medical class to the privileges you intend to exercise.

Book with a GACA-authorized aviation medical examiner, bring identification and any relevant medical history, and renew before it expires. The Fly GACA medical-validity tool estimates your expiry from the issue date, but the certificate and GACAR Part 67 are the authority.

vfr-weather-minimums.name: VFR weather minimums in Saudi Arabia
vfr-weather-minimums.blurb: The flight visibility and distance from cloud you need to fly VFR under GACAR Part 91, and how they change with airspace and altitude.
vfr-weather-minimums.intro: Flying under visual flight rules means staying clear of cloud and keeping enough visibility to see and avoid other traffic and terrain. GACAR Part 91 sets the minimum flight visibility and distance from cloud for VFR, and they change with the class of airspace and your altitude. This guide explains the shape of those minimums and where to confirm the exact figures. It is an educational overview, not the regulation, so always read the current numbers in GACAR Part 91 at gaca.gov.sa.

sections.p: Under visual flight rules you navigate by outside visual reference, so the rules require a minimum flight visibility and a minimum distance from cloud, measured below, above and horizontally, so you can see and avoid other aircraft. These basic VFR weather minimums live in GACAR Part 91 (§91.165). Meeting them is a condition of flying VFR, not a recommendation.

sections.h: They change with airspace and altitude
sections.p: The required visibility and cloud clearance depend on the class of airspace you are in and whether you are above or below certain altitudes. Controlled airspace generally demands more; uncontrolled airspace (Class G) near the surface demands less. The airspace classes themselves are defined in GACAR Part 71. Identify your airspace first, then read the minimum that applies to it.

When a control zone is below the basic VFR minimums, an air traffic control clearance for Special VFR may allow flight clear of cloud with a reduced visibility, at the controller's discretion. It is a clearance you request, not an entitlement, and it carries its own conditions in GACAR Part 91.

Additional limits can apply at night and in some airspace, and VFR flight is not permitted in Class A. Night VFR also interacts with the night-rating and recency rules. Treat the basic minimums as the floor and layer any stricter local or operational limit on top of them.

Get the current weather (METAR/TAF) and forecasts, compare them against the minimum for your route's airspace and altitude, and build a margin. If the numbers are close, the safe answer is often to wait. The Fly GACA VFR minimums and airspace tools help you check, but the regulation is the authority.

pilot-currency-and-recency.name: Pilot currency and recency in Saudi Arabia
pilot-currency-and-recency.blurb: The recent-experience, night, instrument and flight-review rules that keep you legal to fly under GACAR Part 61.
pilot-currency-and-recency.intro: Holding a licence is not the same as being current. Under the GACA Civil Aviation Regulations you must keep recent flight experience and a satisfactory flight review to exercise your privileges, on top of a current medical. This guide explains the kinds of currency GACAR Part 61 tracks and how to stay ahead of them. It is an educational overview, not the regulation, so always confirm the exact figures and intervals in the current GACAR at gaca.gov.sa.

sections.h: Currency is not the same as a valid licence
sections.p: A pilot licence does not lapse the way currency does. To act as pilot in command you also need recent flight experience, a satisfactory flight review, and a current medical certificate under GACAR Part 67. You can hold a perfectly valid licence and still be unable to carry passengers or act as pilot in command until you regain the item you have lost. GACAR Part 61 sets these recency rules.

Before carrying passengers you must have completed a set number of takeoffs and landings within a preceding period, in the same category and class of aircraft, under GACAR Part 61 recent flight experience (§61.17). The exact count and the length of the window are set by the regulation and can change, so read them at source rather than from a summary.

Carrying passengers during the night period adds its own requirement: takeoffs and landings made to a full stop at night. Meeting the daytime requirement does not make you night-current. Check the current definition of the night period and the required count in GACAR Part 61.

To act as pilot in command under instrument flight rules you must have logged recent instrument experience, typically instrument approaches, holding, and intercepting and tracking courses, within a preceding period. If you fall outside it you regain currency by passing an instrument proficiency check with an authorized person. See GACAR Part 61 for the recency rule and Part 91 for the IFR operating rules.

On a recurring interval you must complete a flight review with a GACA-authorized instructor to keep acting as pilot in command. Certain proficiency or licence checks can count in its place. Confirm the current interval and the required content in GACAR Part 61.

Currency is read from your logbook, so record each flight's date, its takeoffs and landings, and your instrument time and approaches. The Fly GACA Part 61 currency and flight-review tools estimate your status from those entries, but the regulation, not the tool, is the authority.

Carrying passengers needs recent takeoffs and landings; night adds a separate full-stop requirement.
Acting as pilot in command under IFR needs recent instrument experience or an instrument proficiency check.
A recurring flight review with an authorized instructor keeps your pilot-in-command privileges alive.

faqs.q: What is a flight review and how often do I need one?
faqs.a: A flight review is a recurring check with a GACA-authorized instructor that you must complete to keep acting as pilot in command; some proficiency or licence checks can satisfy it in place of a standalone review. Confirm the current interval and required content in GACAR Part 61. Fly GACA is an independent study aid and does not conduct reviews or issue licences; GACA is the authority.

how-to-become-a-pilot-in-saudi-arabia.name: How to become a pilot in Saudi Arabia
how-to-become-a-pilot-in-saudi-arabia.blurb: The full path to a Saudi pilot licence, medical, training, exams and the GACAR Parts that govern each step.
how-to-become-a-pilot-in-saudi-arabia.intro: Becoming a pilot in the Kingdom follows a clear path set out in the GACA Civil Aviation Regulations (GACAR). This guide maps the journey end to end, from your first medical to a commercial licence, and links each step to the rule that governs it. It is an educational overview, not a substitute for the regulation: always confirm the current requirements with GACA or an approved training organisation.

sections.p: Decide why you want to fly, for pleasure (a Private Pilot Licence) or for a career (a Commercial, then Airline Transport, licence). You must be old enough for the licence you want, hold a valid aviation medical, and meet the ICAO English language standard. These eligibility rules live in GACAR Part 61.

Hold a medical certificate from a GACA-approved aviation medical examiner, Class 2 is the minimum for a PPL, Class 1 for commercial flying. The medical standards sit in GACAR Part 67, and the certificate has a validity period you must keep current.
Fly with an authorised instructor or Approved Training Organisation (ATO). You build dual and solo hours, including cross-country and night where required, toward the experience the licence demands.

Complete the theoretical-knowledge exams for your licence and pass a practical skill test with an authorised examiner. Ratings such as instrument or night flying are added the same way: training, then a test.

From a PPL you can add an instrument rating, then a Commercial Pilot Licence (with a Class 1 medical and more experience), and ultimately an Airline Transport Pilot Licence for airline command. Each rung raises the hour and standard requirements in Part 61.

how-to-become-a-pilot-in-saudi-arabia.adel: I want to become a pilot in Saudi Arabia. Walk me through the GACAR Part 61 path from medical to commercial licence, and cite the relevant sections.
takeaways: The path is set out in GACAR Part 61 (licensing) and Part 67 (medical).
Start with an aviation medical, Class 2 for a PPL, Class 1 for commercial.
Train with an approved instructor or ATO, then pass theory exams and a skill test.
Add ratings and higher licences (IR → CPL → ATPL) as your experience grows.

faqs.q: How do you become a pilot in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: You train toward a GACA pilot certificate under GACAR Part 61. The usual first step is the private pilot certificate: you must be at least 17 (GACAR §61.133), hold a medical certificate issued after examination by an aviation medical examiner designated under GACAR Part 183 (§67.3), pass the knowledge test on the areas listed in Appendix A to GACAR Part 141, and either graduate an approved course at a Part 141 pilot school or log the required training with an authorized instructor. Fly GACA is an independent educational reference — confirm the current requirements with GACA before you rely on them.

faqs.q: What is the minimum age to start flight training in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.133 requires you to be at least 17 years of age to be issued a private pilot certificate, or at least 16 for a glider or balloon rating. Training can begin earlier; the age applies at issue of the certificate. Fly GACA is independent and educational — verify the current age limits against GACAR Part 61 at gaca.gov.sa.

faqs.q: Do I need a medical certificate before I can fly in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: Yes. GACAR §67.3 requires an applicant for Class 1, Class 2 or Class 3 medical certification to be examined by an aviation medical examiner (AME) designated in accordance with GACAR Part 183. Which class you need depends on the certificate and the operation you are working toward. This is an independent educational summary — confirm the medical class you need with GACA before booking an examination.

faqs.q: Can I train at any flight school in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.133 lets you qualify either by graduating an approved certification course at a pilot school under GACAR Part 141, or by logging the required ground and flight training with an appropriately certificated and rated instructor. Part 141 governs pilot schools and Part 142 governs training centres. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA — check any school's current approval status with GACA directly.

faqs.q: How long does it take to become an airline pilot in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: The regulations set experience, not a calendar. You can hold a commercial pilot certificate from age 18 (GACAR §61.153) and an airline transport pilot certificate from age 23 (§61.173), and an ATP applicant for an airplane category rating needs at least 1,500 hours of total time as a pilot (§61.181). How quickly you build that is a matter of training pace, not regulation. Verify the current requirements against GACAR Part 61 at gaca.gov.sa.

gacar-explained.name: GACAR explained
gacar-explained.blurb: What the Saudi civil-aviation regulations are, how they are organised into Parts, and how to find the rule you need.
gacar-explained.intro: GACAR, the GACA Civil Aviation Regulations, is the body of rules that governs civil aviation in Saudi Arabia. It is organised into numbered Parts, each covering one area, much like the FAA's Federal Aviation Regulations. This guide explains how the library is structured so you can find the exact Part and section that applies. It is an educational overview; the regulation itself is always the authority.

sections.p: GACAR is published by the General Authority of Civil Aviation and carries the force of regulation in the Kingdom. It is modelled on international (ICAO) standards and is closely aligned with the structure of the US FARs, which makes it familiar to pilots trained elsewhere.

The rules are split into numbered Parts. Each Part covers one subject, for example Part 1 holds definitions and abbreviations, Part 61 covers pilot licensing, and Part 91 covers general operating and flight rules. Within a Part, content is divided into subparts and numbered sections.

Identify the subject, open the matching Part, then drill to the subpart and section. A reference like "§61.17" means Part 61, section 17. The library search and Captain Adel both return the exact Part and section so you can verify the wording at source.

Definitions in Part 1 change how every other Part is read, so check a term there first. Always read the current text, regulations are amended over time, and treat summaries (including this one) as a pointer to the rule, never a replacement for it.

gacar-explained.adel: Explain how the GACAR is structured into Parts and how I find a specific rule, with an example citation.
takeaways: GACAR is Saudi Arabia's civil-aviation regulation, organised into numbered Parts.
Each Part covers one subject, e.g. Part 1 definitions, Part 61 licensing, Part 91 operations.
A citation like §61.17 means Part 61, section 17.
Start with Part 1 definitions, and always read the current text at source.

faqs.q: What does GACAR stand for?
faqs.a: GACAR is the General Authority of Civil Aviation Regulations — the body of civil-aviation rules that applies in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The rules are organized into numbered Parts (Part 61 for pilot certification, Part 91 for the general operating and flight rules, and so on), each divided into Subparts and cited by section, such as GACAR §61.133. Fly GACA is an independent educational library, not GACA — read the official text at gaca.gov.sa.

faqs.q: How is GACAR structured?
faqs.a: GACAR is organized into numbered Parts by subject: Part 61 certifies pilots, flight instructors, ground instructors and flight engineers; Part 67 sets medical standards; Part 91 gives the general operating and flight rules; Part 121 covers commercial air operators; Part 141 covers pilot schools. Within a Part, rules are grouped into Subparts and cited by section number (§). This is an independent educational summary — verify any Part against the official text at gaca.gov.sa.

faqs.q: Is GACAR the same as the FAA's FARs?
faqs.a: No. GACAR is Saudi Arabia's own body of civil-aviation regulations, issued by the General Authority of Civil Aviation, and only GACAR applies in the Kingdom. Its Part numbering will look familiar to anyone who has read the US FARs, but the requirements are not identical and you cannot assume a US rule carries over. Fly GACA is independent and not affiliated with GACA — always confirm a requirement in the GACAR text itself.

faqs.q: Which GACAR Part applies to me as a private pilot?
faqs.a: Two apply most directly: GACAR Part 61, which sets how you are certificated and what your privileges and limitations are, and GACAR Part 91, the general operating and flight rules you fly under. Your medical certificate comes from Part 67. Fly GACA is an educational reference, not the regulator — confirm the current text with GACA.

faqs.q: Where can I read the official GACAR text?
faqs.a: The authoritative text is published by the General Authority of Civil Aviation at gaca.gov.sa. Fly GACA is an independent educational library that reproduces and indexes the corpus so you can search it and jump straight to a section, but it never replaces the official text — verify anything you rely on against GACA's published version.

saudi-ppl-requirements.name: Saudi PPL requirements
saudi-ppl-requirements.blurb: What it takes to earn a Private Pilot Licence under GACAR Part 61.
saudi-ppl-requirements.intro: The Private Pilot Licence is the first step to flying for pleasure in the Kingdom. Here is the shape of the path under GACAR Part 61.

sections.p: Be at least 17, hold a current Class 2 medical, and meet the English-language requirement.
Complete the required dual and solo hours with an approved instructor or ATO, including cross-country and night where required.
Pass the theoretical-knowledge exams and the skill test with an authorized examiner.

saudi-ppl-requirements.adel: What are the requirements for a GACAR Part 61 Private Pilot Licence? Cite the section.
takeaways: Minimum age 17, a current Class 2 medical, and ICAO English Level 4.
Train with an approved instructor or ATO, dual, solo, cross-country and night.
Finish with the theory exams and a skill test with an authorized examiner.

faqs.q: What are the requirements for a private pilot licence in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: Under GACAR Part 61 you must be at least 17 years old, hold a current GACA Class 2 medical certificate, and meet the ICAO English requirement (Level 4 or above). You complete dual, solo, cross-country and night training with a GACA-approved instructor or Approved Training Organization (ATO), then pass the theoretical-knowledge examinations and a skill test with an authorized examiner. Always confirm the current requirements against GACAR Part 61 and Part 67 at gaca.gov.sa.

faqs.q: How old do you have to be to get a PPL in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: You must be at least 17 years old to be issued a Private Pilot Licence under GACAR Part 61. You can begin training earlier; the age applies to issue of the licence. Confirm the current minimum age in GACAR Part 61.

faqs.q: What medical certificate do I need for a Saudi PPL?
faqs.a: A current GACA Class 2 medical certificate, issued under the GACAR Part 67 medical standards by a GACA-authorized aviation medical examiner. Check the current standards and validity period in GACAR Part 67.

faqs.q: Do I need English language proficiency for a Saudi PPL?
faqs.a: Yes. You must demonstrate ICAO English language proficiency at Level 4 (Operational) or above through the Saudi aviation English assessment. Verify the current language requirement with GACA.

faqs.q: Where can I train for a PPL in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: You train with a GACA-approved flight instructor or an Approved Training Organization (ATO). Fly GACA is an independent educational study aid — it does not provide flight training or issue licences; GACA is the authority. Confirm approved training providers with GACA.

saudi-cpl-requirements.name: Saudi CPL requirements
saudi-cpl-requirements.blurb: The path from a PPL to a Commercial Pilot Licence.
saudi-cpl-requirements.intro: The Commercial Pilot Licence lets you fly for hire. It builds on the PPL with more experience and stricter standards.

sections.p: Hold a PPL, a current Class 1 medical, and the required English level.
Build the total and specific hours (PIC, cross-country, night, instrument) required by Part 61.
Pass the CPL theory exams and the commercial skill test.

saudi-cpl-requirements.adel: What are the GACAR Part 61 requirements for a Commercial Pilot Licence?
takeaways: Builds on the PPL with a Class 1 medical and more flight experience.
Meet the total and specific hour requirements of Part 61 (PIC, night, instrument).
Pass the CPL theory exams and the commercial skill test.

faqs.q: What are the requirements for a commercial pilot licence in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: Under GACAR §61.153 you must be at least 18 years of age, pass the knowledge test on the aeronautical knowledge areas listed in Appendix C to GACAR Part 141, and either graduate an approved commercial pilot certification course or log the required training for the category and class rating you want. Medical certification is governed by GACAR Part 67. Fly GACA is an independent educational reference — confirm the current requirements with GACA before you rely on them.

faqs.q: How many flight hours do you need for a CPL in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: If you are not graduating from an approved commercial pilot certification course, Appendix D to GACAR Part 61 requires at least 250 hours of flight time as a pilot for an airplane single-engine rating, including at least 200 hours in airplanes and at least 100 hours of pilot-in-command time in airplanes. Graduates of an approved Part 141 course follow that course's requirements instead. This is an independent educational summary — verify the current hours against GACAR Part 61 at gaca.gov.sa.

faqs.q: How much cross-country time does a Saudi CPL need?
faqs.a: Appendix D to GACAR Part 61 requires the 100 hours of pilot-in-command time to include at least 50 hours of cross-country flight, of which at least 20 hours must be in airplanes, for an airplane single-engine rating on the non-approved-course route. Fly GACA is independent and educational — confirm the current experience requirements with GACA.

faqs.q: How old do you have to be for a Saudi commercial pilot licence?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.153 requires you to be at least 18 years of age to be issued a commercial pilot certificate. You may train before then; the age applies at issue. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA — verify the current minimum age in GACAR Part 61.

faqs.q: Do I need instrument training for a Saudi CPL?
faqs.a: Appendix D to GACAR Part 61 requires the non-approved-course applicant to complete at least 20 hours of training on the areas of operation in Appendix C to GACAR Part 141, which includes at least 10 hours of instrument training using a view-limiting device. That is training toward the commercial certificate, and is separate from holding an instrument rating under GACAR §61.89. Confirm the current requirements against GACAR Part 61 at gaca.gov.sa.

saudi-instrument-rating.name: Saudi instrument rating
saudi-instrument-rating.blurb: Adding the rating that lets you fly in cloud.
saudi-instrument-rating.intro: An instrument rating permits flight in instrument meteorological conditions, under IFR.

sections.p: Hold at least a PPL and a valid medical certificate.
Complete instrument instruction and the required instrument time, including approaches.
Pass the instrument theory and the instrument-rating skill test.

saudi-instrument-rating.adel: What does GACAR Part 61 require for an instrument rating?

Pass the instrument theory exam and the instrument skill test.

faqs.q: What are the requirements for an instrument rating in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.89 requires you to hold at least a current private pilot certificate (or apply for one concurrently) with an airplane, helicopter or powered-lift rating appropriate to the instrument rating sought, pass the knowledge test on the areas in Appendix B to GACAR Part 141, complete an approved instrument rating course or the equivalent logged training, and pass the practical test on the Appendix B areas of operation. Fly GACA is an independent educational reference — confirm the current requirements with GACA.

faqs.q: Do I need a private pilot licence before an instrument rating in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: You must hold at least a current private pilot certificate, or be applying for one concurrently, with a category rating appropriate to the instrument rating you want — GACAR §61.89(a)(1). This is an independent educational summary; verify the current prerequisite against GACAR Part 61 at gaca.gov.sa.

faqs.q: Can I do the instrument rating without an approved course?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.89(a)(3) allows three routes: graduating an approved instrument rating course under Appendix B to GACAR Part 141 (or the combined private-plus-instrument course under Appendix L), completing an approved instrument training programme of a GACAR Part 121 air operator, or receiving and logging ground and flight training from an appropriately certificated and rated instructor and meeting the aeronautical experience requirements of Appendix E to Part 61. Fly GACA is independent and educational — confirm which route applies to you with GACA.

faqs.q: Which test do I take for a Saudi instrument rating?
faqs.a: Unless you already hold an instrument rating, GACAR §61.89(a)(2) requires the knowledge test on the aeronautical knowledge areas of Appendix B to GACAR Part 141, and §61.89(a)(4) requires a practical test on the Appendix B areas of operation, flown in an aircraft appropriate to the rating. Verify the current testing requirements with GACA before you book.

faqs.q: Are there restrictions on non-Saudi instructors for instrument training?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.89(a)(3) records that, effective 1 January 2023, appropriately certificated and rated non-Saudi national instructors — except GCC national instructors — must be employed by a GACA certificated pilot school. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA — confirm the current position in GACAR Part 61 at gaca.gov.sa.

faqs.q: Who needs a Class 1 medical in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: Anyone exercising commercial or airline transport pilot privileges needs a valid Class 1 medical; a private pilot (PPL) only needs a Class 2. Check which class your intended privileges require in GACAR Part 67.

faqs.q: What does a Class 1 aviation medical examine?
faqs.a: It assesses vision, hearing, cardiovascular health, neurological and mental fitness, and general physical condition against the GACAR Part 67 standards. The exact tests are set by GACA — verify the current requirements with a GACA-authorized examiner.

faqs.q: How long is a GACA Class 1 medical valid?
faqs.a: The validity is time-limited and generally shortens as you get older. The current periods are set in GACAR Part 67 — confirm your exact validity with GACA, as it depends on your age and the privileges exercised.

faqs.q: Where do I get a GACA Class 1 medical?

faqs.q: What do I need to convert my licence to GACA?
faqs.a: A valid foreign licence, your logbook, a current GACA-accepted medical, photo ID, ICAO English Level 4, and a pass in the GACA air-law examination — with a skill test where required. Verify the exact document list and steps with GACA before applying.

faqs.q: Do I have to retake exams to convert my licence?
faqs.a: You generally sit a GACA air-law examination covering Saudi regulations and demonstrate ICAO English proficiency; a skill test may also be required depending on your licence and ratings. The current requirements are set by GACA under Part 61 — confirm them before you apply.

faqs.q: Do I need a new medical to convert my licence?
faqs.a: Yes — a current GACA medical of the class appropriate to your privileges (Class 1 for commercial/airline, Class 2 for private), under GACAR Part 67. Check the accepted medicals and validity with GACA.

faqs.q: Does Fly GACA convert or issue licences?
faqs.a: No. Fly GACA is an independent educational study aid; it does not process conversions or issue licences. GACA is the authority — apply and confirm all requirements through GACA.

icao-english-saelpt.name: ICAO English & SAELPT
icao-english-saelpt.blurb: The language proficiency requirement for radiotelephony.
icao-english-saelpt.intro: Pilots must demonstrate ICAO English language proficiency at Level 4 (Operational) or above to use English on the radio—a requirement under GACA and GACAR Part 61 licensing rules. The ICAO scale runs from Level 1 (Pre-Elementary) to Level 6 (Expert), and six skill areas are assessed: pronunciation, structure, vocabulary, fluency, comprehension and interactions. Your overall level is the lowest score of the six, so balancing all six is essential. In Saudi Arabia, pilots are tested through the SAELPT—the Saudi Aviation English Language Proficiency Test—which rates you against the ICAO Annex 1 scale. Level 4 allows unrestricted radio communication; higher levels (Level 5 and 6) last longer before re-assessment. Level 4 itself is re-tested periodically—the exact intervals are set by GACA. Passing SAELPT is not optional; it is a prerequisite to holding and exercising a pilot licence to operate on English-language frequencies. Use this guide to understand the six skill areas and begin preparing for your SAELPT assessment.

sections.p: ICAO operational level (Level 4) is required to exercise privileges using English radiotelephony.
Pronunciation, structure, vocabulary, fluency, comprehension and interactions.
Level 4 is re-tested periodically; higher levels last longer.

faqs.q: What is the SAELPT?

faqs.q: What are the ICAO language proficiency levels?
faqs.a: The ICAO scale runs from Level 1 to Level 6, with Level 4 (Operational) the minimum for radio use and Level 6 (Expert) the highest. Six skills are rated and your overall level is the lowest of the six. Confirm how the levels apply to your licence with GACA.

faqs.q: How often do I need to re-test my aviation English?
faqs.a: Level 4 is re-assessed periodically, while higher levels are valid for longer (Level 6 is typically not re-tested). The exact intervals are set by GACA under the ICAO framework — confirm your re-test date with GACA.

faqs.q: How is aviation English scored?
faqs.a: Across six skills — pronunciation, structure, vocabulary, fluency, comprehension and interactions — each rated 1–6; your overall proficiency level is the lowest score of the six. Check the current SAELPT scoring with GACA.

faqs.q: What are the airspace classes in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: GACAR Part 71 defines airspace in the Kingdom as Classes A through G. Class A is below FL 600 only; Class B surrounds major airports; Class C is around medium airports; Class D is around smaller airports; Class E is general controlled airspace; Class F is for when ATC provides no separation; Class G is uncontrolled airspace. Part 71 details the designation and classification of each airspace area. Fly GACA is an independent educational reference — verify the current airspace structure against GACAR Part 71 at gaca.gov.sa.

faqs.q: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled airspace?
faqs.a: In controlled airspace (Classes A, B, C, D and E), GACAR Part 91 requires you to have a clearance before entering and ATC provides separation from other traffic. In uncontrolled airspace (Classes F and G), ATC gives information only; separation is your responsibility. The airspace classification on your sectional chart or in the AIP shows which class applies to your flight route. Fly GACA is educational — confirm the airspace classification for your planned route with an ATC facility or the AIP.

faqs.q: Do I need a clearance to fly in Class E airspace?
faqs.a: GACAR §91.165 sets VFR weather minima for Class E airspace and requires clearance to enter. Class E is the general controlled airspace found above 1,200 feet outside the control zones of Class A, B, C or D airspace and above 700 feet in certain areas. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA — confirm the clearance requirement for your departure aerodrome and route with the local ATC facility.

faqs.q: What VFR weather minima apply in Saudi airspace?
faqs.a: GACAR Part 91 sets VFR minima by airspace class. Class G below 1,000 feet requires 1,500 m visibility and clear of cloud; above 1,000 feet, 5,000 m visibility and 300 m cloud clearance. Class E minima are 5,000 m visibility and 1,000 feet separation from cloud. Classes B, C and D have tighter minima. Exact minima are on your sectional or in GACAR §91.165. Fly GACA is independent — verify the current minima against GACAR Part 91 before your flight.

reading-metar-taf.name: Reading METAR & TAF
reading-metar-taf.blurb: Decode aviation weather reports and forecasts.
reading-metar-taf.intro: METAR and TAF reports pack aviation weather into a compact code—but once you learn the structure, they become quick and reliable. A METAR is an observation of current conditions: wind, visibility, weather, cloud layers, temperature, and pressure. A TAF forecasts the weather over 24 to 30 hours, issued four to six times daily. Both reports follow a fixed field order. The groups FM (from), BECMG (becoming) and TEMPO (temporary) mark when conditions shift in a TAF. Learning to decode them is essential under GACAR Part 91, which governs VFR operations and weather minimums. The field order never changes—whether you're reading from Riyadh or elsewhere, once you recognize the structure, even unfamiliar reports decode systematically. Practice with real observations in a METAR or TAF decoder to build speed and confidence.

A forecast over a validity period, with FM, BECMG and TEMPO change groups.

keyFacts.value: Observation of wind, visibility, weather, cloud layers, temperature, dew point and altimeter setting.

faqs.q: What is a METAR and how do you read it?
faqs.a: A METAR is an aerodrome meteorological report issued regularly (usually hourly) that observes current conditions. It follows a fixed order: station, time, wind (direction and speed), visibility in metres, weather phenomena, cloud layers with ceiling, temperature, dew point and altimeter setting. GACAR Part 91 requires you to be familiar with this format before VFR flight. The Fly GACA METAR decoder translates the code into plain language — use it to practice. Fly GACA is an independent educational reference; verify any report against the original source.

faqs.q: What does a TAF tell you?
faqs.a: A Terminal Aerodrome Forecast (TAF) is a forecast of weather at an aerodrome issued 4 or 6 times daily, valid for 24 or 30 hours ahead. It uses the same format as a METAR but adds change groups: FM (from) marks an abrupt change, BECMG (becoming) marks gradual change, and TEMPO (temporary) marks a brief fluctuation. GACAR Part 91 requires you to understand TAF format before flight planning. Fly GACA is educational; use the Fly GACA TAF decoder and verify the current forecast at your destination.

faqs.q: What do the cloud abbreviations in METAR and TAF mean?
faqs.a: Cloud cover is coded by coverage: SKC (sky clear), FEW (1/8 to 2/8 coverage), SCT (scattered, 3/4 to 4/8), BKN (broken, 5/8 to 7/8), OVC (overcast, 8/8). Each layer also carries a height in hundreds of feet, e.g. 'BKN025' means broken cloud at 2,500 feet. Understanding these codes is essential for VFR flight planning under GACAR Part 91. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA — confirm the current cloud forecast against the official report at your aerodrome.

faqs.q: How often is a METAR issued?
faqs.a: METARs are typically issued every hour at major and medium aerodromes, and every 30 minutes during hazardous conditions. Special METARs (SPECI) may be issued outside the regular cycle when conditions change significantly. GACAR Part 91 requires you to use current weather reports for flight planning. Check the METAR age before you rely on it — reports more than 3 hours old should be treated cautiously. Fly GACA is independent; verify the currency of any METAR with ATC or the aerodrome.

decoding-notams.name: Decoding NOTAMs
decoding-notams.blurb: Make sense of NOTAMs and their Q-codes.
decoding-notams.intro: A NOTAM—Notices to Airmen—alerts pilots to conditions that affect flight safety, operations or airspace. Every NOTAM follows a fixed structure with five key fields: the airport (A), effective date and time (B), expiry date and time (C), the coded alert subject and nature (E and the Q-code), and the plain-language description. The Q-code is a three-part compressed identifier per ICAO Doc 8126 that encodes the issue type (navigation aid status, runway closure, aerodrome hazard), its status, and severity. Reading NOTAMs is required under GACAR Part 91 for flight planning—a missing or misread NOTAM can mean operating into a closed runway or an airfield with a hazard. The field order never changes, which means once you recognize the pattern—even unfamiliar NOTAMs decode systematically. Most importantly, every NOTAM in your planned flight area must be reviewed before departure. Use the NOTAM tool here to expand abbreviations and extract the plain text from the coded format.

Use the NOTAM decoder to expand the abbreviations.

faqs.q: What is a NOTAM and why are they important?
faqs.a: A NOTAM (Notice to Airmen) is an alert to pilots about changes to facilities, services, procedures or hazards that affect a flight. It might warn of a runway closure, navigation aid outage, airspace restriction, or hazard like wind shear. GACAR Part 91 requires you to check NOTAMs for your departure, destination and alternate aerodromes as part of flight planning. Every NOTAM carries an effective date/time and end date/time, so always verify it is current before your flight. Fly GACA is independent; check the real NOTAM service at your aerodrome or the AIP.

faqs.q: What does a Q-code in a NOTAM mean?
faqs.a: The Q-code is a compact 8-character summary of the NOTAM subject and condition, defined by ICAO Doc 8126. The first letter codes the subject (e.g. Q for air navigation facilities, L for lighting, P for parking/apron), and the remaining letters code the condition (e.g. WLY for work on level, CAL for calibration, UU for unserviceable). A Q-code like 'QWFLW' stands for wind shear forecast; 'QPLFM' stands for lighting failure-MALS. Understanding Q-codes saves time in flight planning. Fly GACA is educational; use the NOTAM decoder to expand any unfamiliar code.

faqs.q: How do I know if a NOTAM still applies?
faqs.a: Every NOTAM has an effective date and time (field B) and an end date and time (field C). If the current date and time fall outside that window, the NOTAM is expired and no longer applies. GACAR Part 91 requires you to check NOTAMs as part of preflight planning, so always verify the effective times match your intended flight time. Expired NOTAMs should be disregarded, and any NOTAM you cannot verify as current should be treated as unreliable. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA; confirm active NOTAMs with ATC or your flight service.

faqs.q: What are the main NOTAM abbreviations I need to know?
faqs.a: Common NOTAM abbreviations include: CAT (category), FAC (facility), UNSVCE (unserviceable), OPR (operational), CLG (closed), CAL (calibration), MAINT (maintenance), WIP (work in progress), RWY (runway), NVD (navigation), LGT (lighting), MALS (medium-intensity approach lights), PAPI (precision approach path indicator). Most NOTAMs will use a mix of these and other standard abbreviations. Use the Fly GACA NOTAM decoder or ICAO Doc 8126 to look up unfamiliar abbreviations. Fly GACA is independent; check the authoritative NOTAM service for your flight.

the-airac-cycle.name: The AIRAC cycle
the-airac-cycle.blurb: Why aeronautical data changes every 28 days.
the-airac-cycle.intro: The AIRAC cycle is a fixed 28-day worldwide schedule on which charts, procedures and navigation data update together. The 28-day interval allows time for data production, notification and global implementation. Every effective date falls on a Thursday and applies worldwide, so pilots everywhere switch to new procedures on the same day, keeping operations consistent. The cycle governs all aeronautical information: instrument procedures, departures and arrivals, runway configurations and navigation aid status. GACAR Part 91 requires familiarity with the current AIRAC cycle for flight operations—outdated charts and procedures create confusion and safety risks. The cycle anchors to AIRAC 2001 (effective 2020-01-02) and cycles forward 28 days at a time, so you can always count from a known date. Use the AIRAC tool to check the current cycle number, effective date and countdown to the next.

sections.p: AIRAC effective dates are fixed worldwide, 28 days apart.
Everyone changes to the new data on the same date, so the system stays consistent.
Use the AIRAC tool for the current cycle and the countdown to the next.

the-airac-cycle.adel: What is the AIRAC cycle and why is it 28 days?
takeaways: Aeronautical data updates worldwide on fixed dates 28 days apart.

keyFacts.value: 28 days — the same worldwide, every cycle 28 days after the last effective date.

keyFacts.value: Fixed on Thursdays worldwide; charts, procedures and navigation data change together.

faqs.q: What is the AIRAC cycle?
faqs.a: AIRAC (Aeronautical Information Regulation and Control) is the worldwide schedule on which aeronautical information is published. A new AIRAC cycle begins every 28 days, always on a Thursday, and every chart, procedure, and navigation aid update is effective on the same date worldwide. GACAR Part 91 requires you to use current information, so you must switch to the new cycle on its effective date. The Fly GACA AIRAC tool shows the current cycle number and the date of the next effective publication. Fly GACA is independent; verify the current AIRAC cycle at your aerodrome or with ATC.

faqs.q: Why is the AIRAC cycle exactly 28 days?
faqs.a: The 28-day interval allows time for all the world's aeronautical information producers — chart makers, procedure designers, navigation service providers — to collect changes, coordinate them, and publish updates that all take effect on the same date. This synchronization keeps the global system consistent and prevents pilots from trying to reconcile old and new data. GACAR Part 91 assumes you are using current publications; flying with outdated charts or procedures is a violation. Fly GACA is educational; check the current AIRAC cycle before your flight.

faqs.q: What happens if I use an old chart after a new AIRAC cycle takes effect?
faqs.a: Navigation aids, instrument departures and arrivals, runway configurations, and other critical information change on each AIRAC effective date. If you fly with an out-of-date chart, you may have wrong altitude restrictions, wrong procedure turns, or wrong navigation aid information — all of which create safety risks. GACAR Part 91 requires use of current information; flying with superseded charts is a regulatory violation. Always carry the current edition of your sectional chart or approach plate and confirm the AIRAC cycle before departure. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA; confirm publication currency with ATC.

faqs.q: How often do I need to update my charts?
faqs.a: Charts are typically issued every 56 days (two AIRAC cycles), so each chart covers two cycles. However, some details like low-level wind shear warnings, runway status or special procedures may be published more frequently. The best practice is to check the AIRAC cycle the night before your flight and verify that your paper charts or electronic charts are current. GACAR Part 91 requires current information; running out of chart currency before your flight is your responsibility as pilot in command. Fly GACA is independent; use the AIRAC tool to check if your current publications are still valid.

night-rating.name: Night rating
night-rating.blurb: Adding the privilege to fly after dark.
night-rating.intro: Flying at night brings different rules, lighting, and currency requirements. A night rating—or the night training endorsement—adds the privilege to act as pilot in command after sunset. GACAR §61.135 defines what you can and cannot do at night, and the boundary is sunrise to sunset for day-only pilots. Without night training, a private or commercial pilot may only fly when the sun is above the horizon, which eliminates entire seasons and mission profiles. Night training requires a minimum of 10 hours of dual instruction including 5 hours of night cross-country navigation and 10 full-stop landings. The training covers takeoffs and circuits in darkness, night landing technique (which demands precision—runway lighting is your only visual reference), and navigation when ground features are not visible. After training, you must maintain night currency: carry passengers at night only if you have completed three takeoffs and full-stop landings to a full stop during daylight or civil twilight within the preceding 90 days. Flying at night opens new doors—but only after demonstrated competency.

sections.p: Permission to act as pilot in command at night, beyond the day-only limits of a basic licence.
Dual night instruction covering takeoffs, circuits, landings and night navigation.
Stay night-current by meeting the recent-experience rule before carrying passengers at night.

takeaways: A night rating lifts the day-only limit on a basic licence.
Training covers night takeoffs, circuits, landings and navigation.
Recent-experience rules apply before carrying passengers at night.

keyFacts.label: Without night rating

faqs.q: Can I fly at night without a night rating under GACAR?
faqs.a: No. GACAR §61.135 restricts a private or commercial pilot without night training to flight only during daylight hours — no flight is permitted between sunset and sunrise. To fly at night, you must have completed appropriate night training and obtained the night endorsement. Fly GACA is an independent educational reference; confirm the exact daylight limits with GACA before planning a night flight.

faqs.q: What training is required for night flying in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.135 sets night training requirements for private pilots: at least 10 hours of night flight instruction, of which at least 5 hours must be night navigation including cross-country flight, and at least 10 takeoffs and landings to a full stop at an aerodrome during the period between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise the following day. You must then pass a knowledge test and a practical skill test. Fly GACA is educational; contact an approved training organisation in the Kingdom for current night training requirements.

faqs.q: What is the currency requirement for night flying with passengers?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.17 requires that to carry passengers on a flight at night, you must have completed at least 3 full-stop landings at an aerodrome between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise within the preceding 90 days. If you have not flown three night landings in 90 days, you lose the privilege to carry passengers at night until you restore your currency. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA; verify the current recency requirement in GACAR Part 61.

faqs.q: What time of day counts as night for flying purposes?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.17 defines night as the period between 1 hour after official sunset and 1 hour before official sunrise the following day, determined by the position of the sun relative to the aerodrome location. It is not 'whenever it is dark' — the rules use the sunset/sunrise times for your location. Check official sunset and sunrise times for your departure and destination aerodromes before planning your flight. Fly GACA is independent; use official weather or aerodrome data for accurate sunset/sunrise times.

faqs.a: GACAR §61.173 requires an airline transport pilot certificate applicant to be at least 23 years of age and of good moral character, and to hold a commercial pilot certificate with an instrument rating or an equivalent foreign ATP licence with instrument privileges issued by a Contracting State and carrying no geographical limitations. This is an independent educational summary — verify the current hours against GACAR Part 61 at gaca.gov.sa.

faqs.q: What is the minimum age for an airline transport pilot certificate in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.173(a) requires you to be at least 23 years of age to be issued an ATP certificate. Fly GACA is independent and not affiliated with GACA — confirm the current minimum age in GACAR Part 61.

faqs.q: Can simulator time count toward the Saudi ATPL hours?
faqs.a: Within limits. GACAR §61.181 allows a maximum of 25 hours of training in a full flight simulator representing the class of airplane sought to count toward the 50-hour in-class requirement when accomplished in an approved course under Parts 121, 135, 141 or 142, and caps simulated instrument credit against the 75-hour instrument requirement. Verify the current crediting rules against GACAR Part 61 before you plan around them.

faqs.q: Is there an age limit for flying as an ATP in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.3 provides that a person holding a commercial pilot certificate or airline transport pilot certificate may not serve as a pilot in international operations under GACAR Part 121 or 135 after their 60th birthday, or after their 65th birthday in operations with more than one pilot. Fly GACA is an educational reference, not the regulator — confirm the current limitation with GACA.

flight-instructor-rating.name: Flight instructor rating
flight-instructor-rating.intro: A flight instructor rating (CFII in the US context, or the GACAR equivalent) authorizes you to teach others to fly—and it is one of aviation's most demanding certifications. GACAR Part 61 sets exacting standards because what you teach becomes muscle memory and decision-making reflexes in your students. You must hold a commercial certificate first and typically 250+ flight hours before you qualify to instruct. Training itself spans 25–40 hours: you learn how to teach (not just how to fly), study the principles of learning, practice scenario-based instruction, master the art of critique without criticism, and learn to recognize and recover from emergency situations alongside your student. You must pass a written exam covering teaching methodology, flight physiology, and emergency procedures, then a practical test (checkride) where an examiner watches you teach a student to fly. Your first students won't be strangers—they will be your weakest link, and your instruction will determine whether they become safe pilots or dangerous ones. Currency rules are strict: GACAR requires you to conduct flight instruction at least once every 24 calendar months or you lose the rating. Many instructors shoot for once every 12 months. You must also maintain your own commercial certificate through recurrent training and flight review. The rating expires every two years and renews only through active instruction or passing a re-check. It is a responsibility that never ends: your teaching is your student's foundation.

sections.p: Hold a CPL (or higher) with the ratings you intend to teach and a valid medical.
Learn the fundamentals of instructing, lesson planning, briefing and assessing, and demonstrate teaching from the right seat.
Pass the instructor theory and a skill test that assesses your ability to teach.

takeaways: An instructor rating builds on a commercial licence and its ratings.
Training covers lesson planning, briefing and right-seat flying.
The skill test assesses your ability to teach, not just to fly.

faqs.q: What are the requirements for a flight instructor certificate in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.215 requires you to hold a current commercial pilot certificate or airline transport pilot certificate, pass a knowledge test on flight instructor topics, accumulate at least 250 hours of flight time as pilot in command, have at least 100 hours in the category and class you intend to teach, and pass an oral and practical skill test that assesses your knowledge of fundamentals of instruction and your ability to teach. faqs.q: Can you be a flight instructor with only a private pilot certificate?
faqs.a: No. GACAR §61.215 requires an applicant for a flight instructor certificate to hold at least a commercial pilot certificate. A private pilot cannot give flight instruction for compensation or as part of a training programme under Part 141 or 142, although limited instruction without compensation to family or friends may be permitted. Fly GACA is educational; verify what instruction is allowed by law with GACA before you teach any student.

faqs.q: How many hours do you need to become a flight instructor in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.215 requires a minimum of 250 hours of total flight time as pilot in command, including at least 100 hours in the category and class of aircraft you intend to teach (e.g. single-engine piston aeroplanes). Beyond those minimums, you must also pass a knowledge test and a practical skill test. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA; get your current flight time requirements from an approved training organisation or GACA directly.

faqs.q: What is tested in a flight instructor practical test?
faqs.a: GACAR §61.215 requires the practical test to assess your knowledge of fundamentals of instruction and your ability to teach. You will be examined orally on instructional technique, flight fundamentals, student assessment, and how to correct common errors. The practical component usually involves demonstrating your teaching from the right seat, planning a lesson, and delivering instruction on a manoeuvre or procedure. radiotelephony-phraseology.name: Radiotelephony phraseology
radiotelephony-phraseology.blurb: Standard words that keep the radio clear.
radiotelephony-phraseology.intro: Standard radiotelephony phraseology is essential to aviation safety because the radio is the sole link between you and air traffic control—and noise, accents and distance all make it easy to misunderstand. GACAR Part 91 requires standard phraseology; ICAO Annex 10 defines it. A single misheard clearance can mean flying into an active runway or descending into terrain. Standard phraseology solves this by using exact words with no variation: 'Roger' (message received), 'Wilco' (will comply), 'Say again' (repeat that), 'Read back' (confirm what I heard), 'Affirmative' (yes) and 'Negative' (no). These words have no slang equivalents. Numbers are spoken digit-by-digit (say 'three-two-zero' not 'three-twenty'), and letters are spelled using the phonetic alphabet (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie…) to prevent confusion. Readbacks are critical: when you receive a clearance, read it back exactly, and the controller confirms or corrects it on the spot. This double-check catches mistakes before they become accidents. Non-English-speaking pilots must use the same phonetic alphabet and standard words, which means every pilot worldwide speaks the same radio language. Proficiency in phraseology is as important as aircraft handling—it is your safety net on the radio.

sections.p: Spell letters with Alpha, Bravo, Charlie… so call signs and codes are never confused.
Use words like 'roger', 'wilco', 'say again' and 'readback' with their exact meanings.
Speak numbers clearly and read back clearances so the controller can confirm them.

takeaways: Standard phraseology keeps every call short and unambiguous.
The phonetic alphabet prevents confusion over letters and codes.
Read back clearances so the controller can confirm them.

faqs.q: Why is standard radiotelephony phraseology important?
faqs.a: Standard phraseology prevents misunderstandings on the radio. A non-standard call may not be understood, or the listener may interpret it differently than you intended, creating safety risks. GACAR Part 91 requires you to use standard phraseology, defined by ICAO Annex 10. Using the phonetic alphabet for letters (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie) and specific words with precise meanings (Roger, Wilco, Say again) ensures every call is unambiguous and clear. Fly GACA is independent; learn the full standard phraseology from an approved flight school or the GACA radio operator handbook.

faqs.q: What does 'Roger' mean in aviation radio?
faqs.a: Roger means 'I have received your last transmission and understand it.' It does not mean you will comply with a clearance — that is 'Wilco' (will comply). Roger simply confirms you heard and understood. GACAR Part 91 requires use of standard words, so never say 'Copy' or 'OK' instead of Roger — the controller expects the standard term. Fly GACA is educational; use only the standard phraseology defined by ICAO Annex 10.

faqs.q: Do I have to use the phonetic alphabet on the radio?
faqs.a: Yes. GACAR Part 91 requires that when spelling call signs, aircraft registration or codes where clarity is critical, you use the ICAO phonetic alphabet (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, etc.). This prevents confusion — the letter B and D sound similar on a crackling radio, but Bravo and Delta are unmistakable. Always use the phonetic alphabet for your aircraft registration and any numbers that might be misheard. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA; memorize the phonetic alphabet before your first flight.

faqs.q: What clearances must you always read back?
faqs.a: GACAR Part 91 and ICAO Annex 10 require you to read back all clearances involving altitude, heading, speed, transponder code, and any other clearance that could create safety issues if misunderstood. The controller will confirm your readback. Never assume you understood correctly — always read back to give the controller a chance to catch any errors. If the controller doesn't correct your readback, the clearance has been confirmed. Fly GACA is independent; use standard readback format to avoid confusion.

drone-uas-rules-in-ksa.blurb: Flying unmanned aircraft legally in Saudi Arabia.
drone-uas-rules-in-ksa.intro: Unmanned aircraft are regulated too. In the Kingdom, registration, authorisation and operating limits apply before you fly a drone.

Respect height limits, keep clear of aerodromes and controlled airspace, and avoid restricted areas.
Keep the drone in sight, fly within the stated limits, and follow the small-UAS rules in Part 107.

takeaways: Register and get authorisation before flying a drone in the Kingdom.
Stay clear of aerodromes, controlled airspace and restricted areas.
Keep it in sight and within the Part 107 operating limits.
drone-uas-rules-in-ksa.adel: What are the rules for flying a small drone in Saudi Arabia under Part 107?

keyFacts.label: What counts as small
