faqs.q: What are the drone rules in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: Civil small unmanned aircraft systems are governed by GACAR Part 107, which applies to the registration, airman certification and operation of civil small UAS within the Kingdom (§107.1). Operating limitations in §107.59 include a maximum ground speed of 87 knots (160 km/h) and a maximum altitude of 400 feet (120 m) above ground level, and §107.37 requires the aircraft to stay in unaided visual line of sight. Fly GACA is an independent educational reference — confirm the current rules with GACA before you fly.

faqs.q: How high can you legally fly a drone in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: GACAR §107.59(b) limits a small unmanned aircraft to 400 feet (120 metres) above ground level, unless it is flown within a 400-foot (120 m) radius of a structure, in which case it may not fly higher than 400 feet above that structure's immediate uppermost limit. This is an independent educational summary — verify the current limit against GACAR Part 107 at gaca.gov.sa.

faqs.q: Do I need a licence to fly a drone in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: GACAR Part 107 covers airman certification for civil small UAS, and §107.65 requires an applicant for a remote pilot certificate with a small UAS rating to be at least 18 years of age, to be cleared through the GACA Aviation Security Division, and to be able to read, speak, write and understand English. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA — confirm the current certification requirements and any registration steps with GACA directly.

faqs.q: What counts as a small drone under Saudi rules?
faqs.a: GACAR Part 107 defines a small unmanned aircraft as an unmanned aircraft weighing less than 25 kilograms on takeoff, including everything that is on board or otherwise attached to the aircraft. Heavier or different unmanned operations fall outside Part 107. Verify the current definition against GACAR Part 107 before assuming your aircraft qualifies.

faqs.q: Do I have to keep my drone in sight in Saudi Arabia?
faqs.a: Yes. GACAR §107.37 requires the remote pilot in command, the visual observer if one is used, and the person manipulating the flight controls to be able to see the small unmanned aircraft with vision unaided by any device other than corrective lenses. Fly GACA is an educational reference, not the regulator — confirm the current visual line-of-sight rule with GACA.

weight-and-balance-basics.name: Weight & balance basics
weight-and-balance-basics.intro: Every aircraft has strict weight and centre-of-gravity (CG) limits. Exceeding either compromises controllability, stall behaviour and performance—risking the flight itself. GACAR Part 91 requires the pilot to ensure the aircraft is loaded within weight and CG limits before every departure. Weight limits include the maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) and maximum landing weight (MLW)—published in the aircraft's POH. Centre of gravity describes where the aircraft's balance point lies between forward and aft limits; an out-of-limits CG makes the aircraft difficult to control, changes how it stalls, and alters pitch stability. Loading the aircraft is your responsibility as pilot-in-command, and the numbers must be calculated precisely—not guessed. The loading chart or weight-and-balance tool shows how much you can carry of fuel, payload and passengers before hitting a limit. Running the calculation before any flight that loads near the limits is not optional; it is a regulatory requirement. The weight-and-balance tool here helps you verify your loading is compliant.

sections.p: Stay at or below the maximum take-off and landing weights for the aircraft.
Keep the CG within the forward and aft limits for safe handling and stall behaviour.
Use the loading chart or the weight-and-balance tool before every flight that is close to limits.

takeaways: Respect both the weight limits and the CG envelope.
An out-of-limits CG changes stability and stall behaviour.
Run the numbers before any flight that loads near the limits.
weight-and-balance-basics.adel: Why must a flight stay within its weight and centre-of-gravity limits?

keyFacts.label: Governing rules
keyFacts.value: GACAR Part 91 requires the pilot to ensure the aircraft is loaded within weight and CG limits.

keyFacts.label: Weight limits
keyFacts.value: Maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) and maximum landing weight (MLW) — never exceed these or performance and controllability are compromised.

keyFacts.label: Centre of gravity
keyFacts.value: The CG must remain between the forward and aft limits published for the aircraft; an aft CG reduces stability.

keyFacts.label: Computation
keyFacts.value: Use the aircraft loading chart or the weight-and-balance tool to calculate total weight and CG location before flight.

keyFacts.label: Responsibility
keyFacts.value: The pilot in command is responsible for ensuring the aircraft is loaded within limits before takeoff.

faqs.q: Why does weight and balance matter in an aircraft?
faqs.a: Weight affects how fast the aircraft accelerates, climbs and descends; centre of gravity affects how it handles and stalls. If the total weight exceeds the maximum takeoff weight, the aircraft may not fly, or may run out of runway during takeoff. If the CG is too far aft, the aircraft becomes unstable and difficult to control. If the CG is too far forward, the controls become heavy. GACAR §91.9 requires the pilot in command to ensure the aircraft is loaded within both weight and CG limits. Fly GACA is independent; use the aircraft's loading chart to calculate weight and balance for every flight.

faqs.q: What happens if you load an aircraft beyond its maximum weight?
faqs.a: An overweight aircraft will take longer to accelerate, may not reach flying speed before running out of runway, and may have poor climb performance even if it does fly. Its handling may feel sluggish, and its stall speed is higher, requiring a longer landing distance. GACAR §91.9 prohibits operating an aircraft beyond its maximum takeoff or landing weight. Flying overweight violates the regulation and creates safety risks. Fly GACA is educational; always calculate the total weight including fuel, passengers and baggage before departing.

faqs.q: What is the centre of gravity and why does it matter?
faqs.a: The centre of gravity (CG) is the point where all the aircraft's weight is balanced. An aft CG (toward the tail) reduces longitudinal stability and raises the stall speed; a forward CG (toward the nose) makes the controls heavy but provides stability. GACAR §91.9 requires loading within the manufacturer's CG envelope, published in the aircraft's weight-and-balance document. Loading outside this envelope creates dangerous handling characteristics. Use the loading chart to verify CG before every flight, especially when carrying heavy baggage or passengers. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA; use the Fly GACA weight-and-balance tool for calculations.

faqs.q: How do you calculate weight and balance?
faqs.a: Use the aircraft's loading chart or the Fly GACA weight-and-balance tool: list the empty weight and CG of the aircraft, add each person's weight times their arm (distance from reference point), add fuel weight times its arm, add baggage weight times its arm, total the weights and moments, then divide total moments by total weight to find the CG location. Plot this on the CG envelope graph to verify it falls within limits. GACAR §91.9 requires this calculation before flight; if your calculation shows the CG is outside limits, you must reposition the load or remove weight. Fly GACA is independent; an approved flight school can teach you the calculation method.

density-altitude-and-performance.name: Density altitude & performance
density-altitude-and-performance.blurb: Why hot, high and humid days hurt performance.
density-altitude-and-performance.intro: Density altitude is the altitude your aircraft *feels* it is flying at, even though your altimeter shows a lower number. It combines temperature, pressure, and humidity into a single measure of how thin the air is, and thin air means less lift and less engine power. GACAR Part 91 requires you to account for density altitude in your aircraft's performance calculations before every flight. Here's why it matters: a Cessna 172 needs maybe 1,500 feet of runway to take off on a cool sea-level day. At 5,000 feet elevation on a hot day, the same aircraft might need 3,000 feet—and if your runway is only 2,500 feet long, you cannot safely depart, no matter how short the runway looks. Your aircraft's POH (Pilot's Operating Handbook) contains performance charts that convert actual pressure altitude and temperature into density altitude; from there, you look up the runway distance required, climb rate, and cruise performance at that density altitude. High elevation + high temperature = very high density altitude. Flying over mountains on a hot day? Density altitude could be 2,000 feet higher than your elevation. You may not have the performance you think you have. Performance degradation is insidious because the airplane flies normally—controls feel normal, airspeed is what you expect—but you climb slower, accelerate slower, and use more runway to take off. Respect your aircraft's limits on hot days at high elevations: calculate density altitude, check your performance charts, and do not press marginal runways.

sections.p: The altitude the air 'feels like' to the wing and engine after correcting for temperature.
High density altitude lengthens the take-off roll, flattens the climb and reduces engine power.
Plan with the performance charts, reduce weight, and use the cooler part of the day.

takeaways: Density altitude rises with heat, altitude and humidity.
It lengthens the take-off run and reduces climb performance.
Use performance charts and fly in cooler conditions to manage it.
density-altitude-and-performance.adel: How does density altitude affect take-off and climb performance?

keyFacts.label: Definition
keyFacts.value: Pressure altitude corrected for temperature; the altitude at which the air has that density.

keyFacts.label: Causes
keyFacts.value: High temperature, high altitude, high humidity all increase density altitude.

keyFacts.label: Effect on takeoff
keyFacts.value: Longer takeoff distance required; the engine produces less power and the wing generates less lift in thinner air.

keyFacts.label: Effect on climb
keyFacts.value: Climb performance is degraded; the climb rate decreases significantly at high density altitude.

keyFacts.label: Planning
keyFacts.value: Always use performance charts entered with temperature, altitude and weight to determine required runway and climb capability.

faqs.q: What is density altitude?
faqs.a: Density altitude is the altitude at which the air has the density you are experiencing. It is calculated from pressure altitude and temperature: as temperature rises or pressure drops (altitude increases), the air becomes thinner and density altitude increases. GACAR Part 91 requires you to understand density altitude for flight planning. At the same elevation, a 30-degree day has much higher density altitude than a 10-degree day, so performance is worse. Use the Fly GACA density altitude tool or the aircraft's performance charts to calculate the density altitude for your planned flight.

faqs.q: Why does density altitude affect aircraft performance?
faqs.a: Aircraft engines produce power and wings generate lift based on the density of the air they are moving through. In thinner air (high density altitude), the engine produces less power, the propeller is less efficient, and the wing needs higher speed to produce the same lift. This means longer takeoff distance, reduced climb rate, and longer landing distance. GACAR Part 91 requires flight planning that accounts for density altitude and available runway/field length. In Saudi Arabia's hot climate, density altitude can be dramatically higher than field elevation, especially on summer afternoons. Fly GACA is independent; use the aircraft's performance charts to plan conservatively.

faqs.q: How do you calculate density altitude?
faqs.a: Use the Fly GACA density altitude calculator or the aircraft's performance charts. Enter the aerodrome elevation (pressure altitude if altitude is set to 29.92 inches), the outside air temperature, and dew point. The calculator shows the density altitude and its effect on takeoff and climb performance. Some charts use a slide rule or table method. GACAR §91.105 requires flight planning that includes performance, so calculate density altitude before every flight, especially on hot days or from high aerodromes. Fly GACA is educational; learn both methods so you can calculate DA without a calculator if needed.

faqs.q: What can you do to improve performance on a high-density-altitude day?
faqs.a: Reduce aircraft weight by carrying less fuel (but maintain legal reserves), reducing baggage, or carrying fewer passengers. Depart early in the day when temperature is lower and density altitude is reduced. Use a longer runway if available. If the aircraft cannot meet the performance required, delay the flight until conditions improve. GACAR §91.105 requires flight planning that ensures the aircraft can safely depart and arrive at planned aerodromes, so never attempt to force an overloaded aircraft to depart on a high-DA day. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA; use conservative performance estimates and never exceed published limits.

fuel-planning-and-reserves.name: Fuel planning & reserves
fuel-planning-and-reserves.blurb: How much fuel the rules require you to carry.
fuel-planning-and-reserves.intro: Fuel planning is the foundation of safe flight operations: you must calculate how much fuel you need, how much you have, and where you will go if the planned destination becomes unreachable. GACAR Part 91 and Part 121 require documented fuel planning before every flight. The calculation starts with measuring your aircraft's fuel capacity, usually in gallons or litres—check your aircraft's POH (Pilot's Operating Handbook) for the exact quantity. Next, calculate fuel burn: how fast your engines consume fuel at your planned altitude and power setting (typically 8–12 gallons per hour for a Cessna 172 at cruise; your POH gives the exact number for your aircraft). Then multiply burn rate by planned flight time to get fuel required to reach your destination. But fuel required is never fuel to depart with. GACAR requires reserve fuel—fuel you will *not* burn, but carry as a safety margin in case you need to divert, hold in a holding pattern, or execute a missed approach. VFR reserves are typically 30 minutes of fuel; IFR reserves are typically 45 minutes. Total fuel to depart is fuel required plus reserves. Check this total against your aircraft's usable fuel capacity; if reserves exceed capacity, the flight is unflyable. Endurance—how long you can fly on total available fuel—must always exceed flight time plus reserve time. This discipline keeps you airborne long enough to reach an alternate if needed.

sections.p: Fuel to taxi, take off, climb, cruise, descend and land at the destination.
Add contingency, alternate and final-reserve fuel as the operating rules require.
IFR and commercial flights carry extra alternate and holding fuel, see Part 91 and Part 121.

takeaways: Always plan trip fuel plus the required reserves, never just trip fuel.
IFR and commercial operations carry alternate and holding fuel.
Final-reserve fuel is a floor you should never plan to use.
fuel-planning-and-reserves.adel: What are the minimum fuel reserve requirements under GACAR Part 91?

keyFacts.label: VFR reserves
keyFacts.value: 30 minutes of fuel reserve after reaching destination, or 45 minutes if flight is not direct route.

keyFacts.label: IFR reserves
keyFacts.value: 45 minutes of fuel reserve after landing at alternate aerodrome, plus fuel to climb to cruise altitude.

keyFacts.label: Trip fuel
keyFacts.value: Calculated from planned route, expected fuel burn, headwind/tailwind correction, weight and temperature.

keyFacts.label: Alternate aerodrome
keyFacts.value: IFR flights must carry fuel to reach and land at a suitable alternate, plus 45 minutes reserve.

keyFacts.label: Commercial operations
keyFacts.value: GACAR Part 121 and 135 set higher reserve requirements for air transport and charter flights.

faqs.q: How much fuel reserves must you carry for a VFR flight?
faqs.a: GACAR §91.167 requires you to carry at least 30 minutes of fuel reserve after reaching your destination aerodrome, or 45 minutes if the intended route is not a direct route to the destination. This means you must arrive at the destination with at least that much usable fuel remaining in the tanks. This reserve is separate from the trip fuel calculated for your planned route. Fly GACA is an independent educational reference; always calculate reserves conservatively and account for headwind and deteriorating conditions.

faqs.q: What fuel reserves are required for an IFR flight?
faqs.a: GACAR §91.167 requires you to carry fuel to reach the destination, then to climb to cruise altitude and fly to a suitable alternate aerodrome, then to land at the alternate with at least 45 minutes of fuel remaining. You must identify the alternate aerodrome and plan that it meets the weather minima for landing when you arrive. If no suitable alternate is available, you cannot depart. Commercial IFR flights (Part 121 and 135) carry higher reserves. Fly GACA is educational; check the fuel requirements with ATC or a flight planner before departing.

faqs.q: What is 'trip fuel' and how is it different from reserves?
faqs.a: Trip fuel is the fuel needed to fly from departure to destination, including taxi, takeoff, climb, cruise, descent and landing. Reserves are fuel that remains in the tanks after landing, a legal minimum that you carry but do not plan to burn except in an emergency. GACAR §91.105 requires flight planning that calculates trip fuel accurately, and §91.167 sets the minimum reserves. Always plan with conservative assumptions about wind and fuel burn. Fly GACA is not affiliated with GACA; use aircraft performance charts and weather forecasts to calculate trip fuel realistically.

faqs.q: When is an alternate aerodrome required?
faqs.a: GACAR §91.167 requires an alternate aerodrome for IFR flights unless the destination forecast is above minimums for the entire flight time plus 1 hour. The alternate must be within a reasonable distance (usually 30-60 minutes) and forecast to be above minimums when you arrive. VFR flights do not require an alternate by regulation, but good planning means knowing where you can land if weather deteriorates or an emergency occurs. Fly GACA is independent; always identify at least one suitable alternate and plan your fuel load to reach it safely.

criticalPoint.diagramEtpPnr: ETP {{etp}} NM, PNR {{pnr}} NM of {{total}} NM
criticalPoint.formula: The equal time point (ETP) is where continuing and returning take the same time: distance = D·GSh/(GSo+GSh). The point of no return (PNR) is the farthest you can go and still return within your usable endurance E: time = E·GSh/(GSo+GSh). A planning aid: use your operator’s fuel policy.

topOfClimb.formula: Time = altitude to gain ÷ rate of climb; distance = groundspeed × time; fuel = fuel flow × time. Uses an average climb rate, the AFM/POH climb tables are authoritative.

turnPerf.formula: Rate of turn (°/s) = 1091 × tan(bank) ÷ TAS; radius (ft) = TAS² ÷ (11.26 × tan(bank)), with TAS in knots. A steeper bank and a lower speed tighten the turn.

pivotalAlt.formula: Pivotal altitude (ft) = groundspeed (kt)² ÷ 11.3, the height at which the line of sight to a ground reference stays on the wingtip in eights-on-pylons. It rises and falls with groundspeed through the turn.

trueAlt.formula: Correction (ft) ≈ 4 × ISA deviation × (height above the altimeter-setting source ÷ 1,000); true altitude = indicated + correction. Warmer than ISA → you are higher than indicated; colder → lower. An approximation; for terrain-critical cold-weather operations use the AIP/ICAO tables.
